stem: Define: Green chemistry. Write two advantages of nanoparticle and nanotechnology.
solution:
**Green chemistry :** Green chemistry is the use of chemistry for pollution prevention by environmentally conscious design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use or generation of hazardous substances (section 16.1). Put more simply, it is an approach to chemistry that aims to maximize efficiency and minimize hazardous effects on human health and the environment. The concept was coined by Paul T. Anastas, who also enunciated its twelve principles.

**Two advantages of nanoparticles and nanotechnology** (section 16.10) :

1. **Electronics and computing :** nanotechnology has brought about a revolution in electronics and computing.

2. **Medical field :** it allows the manufacture of smart drugs, which help cure faster and without side effects, and helps in the curing of life threatening diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

The chapter lists one more advantage under the same heading, in the energy sector : nanotechnology will make solar power more economical and will make energy storage devices more efficient.

stem: What is atom economy? Explain any two applications of nanomaterials.
solution:
**Atom economy** is principle 2 of green chemistry (section 16.3). It is a measure of the amount of atoms from the starting materials that are present in the useful products at the end of a chemical process. Good atom economy means most of the atoms of the reactants are incorporated into the desired product and only small amounts of unwanted by-products are formed, so there are fewer problems of waste disposal. It is calculated as

\(\% \text{ atom economy} = \dfrac{\text{Formula weight of the desired product}}{\text{sum of formula weight of all the reactants used in the reaction}} \times 100\)

For the chapter's own example, the conversion of butan-1-ol to 1-bromobutane,

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH} + \mathrm{NaBr} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2\text{-}Br} + \mathrm{NaHSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

the desired product supplies \((4\mathrm{C} + 9\mathrm{H} + 1\mathrm{Br}) = 137\ \mathrm{u}\) and the reactants together supply \((4\mathrm{C} + 12\mathrm{H} + 5\mathrm{O} + 1\mathrm{Br} + 1\mathrm{Na} + 1\mathrm{S}) = 275\ \mathrm{u}\), so

\(\% \text{ atom economy} = \dfrac{137\ \mathrm{u}}{275\ \mathrm{u}} \times 100 = 49.81\ \%\)

**Two applications of nanomaterials** (section 16.9) :

1. **Water purification :** water contains waterborne pathogens such as viruses and bacteria, and cost effective filter materials coated with silver nanoparticles (AgNps) are used, for example in a domestic water purifier. The silver nanoparticles act as a highly effective bacterial disinfectant and remove *E. coli* from the water.

2. **Self cleaning materials :** the lotus plant (*Nelumbo nucifera*) grows in muddy water and yet its leaves always appear clean, because they are superhydrophobic. Nanostructures on the lotus leaves repel water, which carries the dirt away with it as it rolls off. This lotus effect is the basis of self cleaning windows.

stem: Write the name of the technique used to know geometry of nanoparticles.
solution:
The technique is **X-ray diffraction (XRD)**, carried out on an X-ray diffractometer.

Table 16.1 of section 16.7.3 lists each characterization technique against the information it yields, and against X-ray diffraction it records "particle size, crystal structure, geometry". It is the only entry in that table whose information column names geometry, so it is the technique that gives the geometry of nanoparticles.

The other techniques in the same table give different information : UV-visible spectroscopy gives preliminary confirmation that nanoparticles have formed, scanning electron microscopy gives the structure of the surface of the material that is its morphology, transmission electron microscopy gives particle size, and FTIR gives absorption by functional groups and binding nature.

Section 16.10 sets out the disadvantages of nanotechnology. Despite the possibilities and the advancements that nanotechnology offers to the world, there also exist certain potential risks involved with it.

1. **Nano pollution :** nanotechnology has raised the standard of living, but at the same time it has increased pollution, which includes air pollution. The pollution caused by nanotechnology is known as nano pollution, and this kind of pollution is very dangerous for living organisms.

2. **Lung damage :** nanoparticles can cause lung damage. Inhaled particulate matter can be deposited throughout the human respiratory tract and then deposit in the lungs. The characteristics of nanoparticles that are relevant for health effects are their size, chemical composition and shape.

stem: The name of metal nanoparticle \(which\ \text{acts}\) as a highly effective bacterial disinfectant in water purification process is _____.
solution:
**(B)** silver

Section 16.9 (c) describes the role of nanotechnology in water purification. Water contains waterborne pathogens such as viruses and bacteria, and the chapter records that cost effective filter materials coated with **silver nanoparticles (AgNps)** are a recent alternative technology, used for example in a domestic water purifier. It then states plainly that silver nanoparticles act as a highly effective bacterial disinfectant and remove *E. coli* from water.

This works because of the characteristic feature described in section 16.6.2 : a nanoparticle has a very high surface-to-volume ratio, so the same mass of silver spread over the filter presents an enormously larger reactive surface to the water passing through it than bulk silver would.

The other three metals and materials named are given other roles by this chapter and none of them is a disinfectant. Carbon black is the nanostructured material used in the tyres of a car to increase the life of the tyre (section 16.8); gold nanoparticles are named for the ruby red colour of ancient glass paintings and for the colour change at nanoscale in section 16.6.1; copper is named only in section 16.6.5, where nanosized copper and palladium clusters are cited for mechanical hardness.

stem: Write the name of metal nanoparticle used to remove E.coli bacteria from water.
solution:
The metal nanoparticle is **silver**, used as silver nanoparticles (AgNps).

Section 16.9 (c) states that cost effective filter materials coated with silver nanoparticles are an alternative technology for water purification, for example in a domestic water purifier, and that silver nanoparticles act as a highly effective bacterial disinfectant and remove *E. coli* from water.

A nanoparticle has a very high surface-to-volume ratio (section 16.6.2), so when a bulk material is subdivided into individual nanoparticles the total volume remains the same while the collective surface area is largely increased. The same mass of silver therefore presents a far larger reactive surface to the water passing through the filter than bulk silver would, which is why the disinfecting action is effective at so small a loading.

stem: What is nano material? Write the reaction involved in sol-gel process during hydrolysis.
solution:
**Nanomaterial :** a nanomaterial is a material having structural components with at least one dimension in the nanometer scale, that is \(1\text{-}100\ \mathrm{nm}\) (section 16.5 d). Nanomaterials are larger than single atoms but smaller than bacteria and cells, and may be nanoparticles, nanowires or nanotubes according to their dimensions. Nanostructured materials may be large organic molecules, inorganic cluster compounds or metallic or semiconductor particles.

**The hydrolysis step of the sol-gel process** (section 16.7.2). The sol-gel process is based on inorganic polymerization reactions and includes four steps : hydrolysis, polycondensation, drying and thermal decomposition. The reaction involved during hydrolysis is written by the chapter as

\(\mathrm{MOR} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{MOH} + \mathrm{ROH}\)

where \(\mathrm{MOR}\) is the metal alkoxide, \(\mathrm{M}\) the metal, \(\mathrm{OR}\) the alkoxide group and \(\mathrm{ROH}\) the alcohol released.

The metal alkoxide is thus attacked by water, the alkoxide group leaves as an alcohol and a metal hydroxide is formed. That hydroxide is what goes on to the next step, condensation, in which

\(\mathrm{MOH} + \mathrm{ROM} \longrightarrow \mathrm{M\text{-}O\text{-}M} + \mathrm{ROH}\)

builds the oxide-bridged network of the gel.

stem: Predict the type of cubic lattice of a solid element having edge length of 400 pm and density is 6.25 g/ml (Atomic mass of element = 60). Define: Nanoscience.
solution:
**Type of cubic lattice.**

Given : edge length \(a = 400\ \mathrm{pm} = 400 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm} = 4 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\), density \(\rho = 6.25\ \mathrm{g/mL} = 6.25\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\), molar mass \(M = 60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).

The density of a cubic crystal in terms of the number of particles \(n\) per unit cell is

\(\rho = \dfrac{n M}{a^3 N_A}\)

so, rearranging for \(n\),

\(n = \dfrac{\rho\, a^3 N_A}{M}\)

The volume of the unit cell is

\(a^3 = \left(4 \times 10^{-8}\right)^3 = 64 \times 10^{-24} = 6.4 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

Substituting,

\(n = \dfrac{6.25 \times 6.4 \times 10^{-23} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}}{60} = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-22} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}}{60} = \dfrac{240.88}{60} = 4.01 \approx 4\)

\(\therefore\) there are 4 particles per unit cell, and a cubic unit cell containing 4 particles is **face-centred cubic (fcc)**.

Check : putting \(n = 4\) back into the density expression gives \(\rho = \dfrac{4 \times 60}{6.4 \times 10^{-23} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}} = 6.23\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\), against the \(6.25\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\) given, so the answer is consistent. The alternatives are far away : \(n = 2\) (bcc) would require \(3.11\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\) and \(n = 1\) (simple cubic) only \(1.56\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\).

**Nanoscience :** nanoscience is the study of phenomena and manipulation of materials at atomic, molecular and macromolecular scales, where properties differ significantly from those at a larger scale (section 16.5 a).

stem: One dimensional nanostructure amongst the following is _____.
solution:
Section 16.5 (d) of the chapter gives the classification and its definition : "A one dimensional nanostructure is one in which two dimensions are in the nanoscale", with the examples nanowires and nano rods; a zero dimensional structure is one in which all three dimensions are in the nanoscale, for example nanoparticles; and a two-dimensional nanostructure is one in which one dimension is in the nanoscale, for example thin films.

Applying that definition to the four alternatives :

- **Nanoparticles** have all three dimensions in the nanoscale, so they are a zero-dimensional nanostructure. Excluded.
- **Nanofilms** are thin films, in which only the thickness is in the nanoscale, so they are a two-dimensional nanostructure. Excluded.
- **Nanorods** have two dimensions in the nanoscale and one that is not, so they satisfy the definition. The chapter names them : its 1-D examples are "Nanowires and Nano rods", and the caption of Fig. 16.15 reads "(b) 1D nanofibers, wires and rods".
- **Nanotubes** likewise have two dimensions in the nanoscale, the diameter, and one that is not, the length, so they satisfy the same definition. The chapter names them too : the table set beside Fig. 16.3 places "Nanotubes, fibres, nanowires" in the one-dimensional row, between the row holding nanoparticles and quantum dots and the row holding thin films, layers and coatings.

**Both nanotubes and nanorods are therefore one-dimensional nanostructures, and this chapter says so of each of them.** The question as printed admits two correct answers, so no single one is recorded here; a student who wrote either has answered correctly. The two that can be settled are nanoparticles and nanofilms, and both are wrong.

stem: Write the name of nano structured material used in car tyres to increase the life of tyres.
solution:
The nanostructured material is **carbon black**.

Section 16.8 lists it among the nanostructured materials that have been in use for a long time : "Carbon black is a nanostructured material that is used in tyres of car to increase the life of tyre. (Discovery in 1900)."

The same list names the other long-standing nanostructured materials for contrast : gold and silver nanoparticles trapped in a glass matrix give the ruby red colour of some ancient glass paintings, spherical metallic nanoparticles give the lustre on some medieval pottery, and fumed silica is a component of silicone rubber, coatings, sealants and adhesives. None of these is used in tyres.
